Bisected and seems like issue started after https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135395/changes/5ff323de791df88880f6e065f5de4b445e5c90ed

So you can reproduce locally via `stress`?

/cc @michaelasp

@akhilerm: how did you bisect?

I can't reproduce with `stress ./cache.test -test.run=TestSharedInformerHandlerAbuse`, not even when increasing the parallelism (`-p 1024`).

Reproduced with 
```
stress -p 16 /tmp/cache_test.bin -test.run TestSharedInformerHandlerAbuse -test.timeout 60s
```
also with timeout of 600s, the same as when it failed in the publishing-bot tests.

I can reproduce it by lowering the test timeout:

```console
$ make WHAT=./staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/cache.test
...
$ stress -p 16 ./_output/local/bin/linux/amd64/cache.test -test.run TestSharedInformerHandlerAbuse -test.timeout 60s
...
1m45s: 4495 runs so far, 6 failures (0.13%)
```

You were using Windows, right? I don't think it matters, just calling it out as something that could have made a difference.

To me that looks like a (minor?) performance degradation in a non-typical stress test. If this was a genuine bug like a deadlock, then it should also fail with a higher timeout.

@michaelasp: what do you think?

When using `stress -p 16` it's possible to compare the performance.

With 5ff323de791:
```
2m0s: 3769 runs so far, 0 failures
```

With 59cddedb04dcb2c3c5550e9f508b9771ba99f29c (base of my branch):
```
2m0s: 3738 runs so far, 0 failures
```

Hmm, no real difference. It actually was a bit faster with the newer code.

> You were using Windows, right? I don't think it matters, just calling it out as something that could have made a difference.

Not windows, on mac M1.

> To me that looks like a (minor?) performance degradation in a non-typical stress test. If this was a genuine bug like a deadlock, then it should also fail with a higher timeout.

I am not sure then why we are hitting it randomly in the publishing-bot runs. I think around 6 times  in the past 2 weeks.

It also occurs on ppc64le: https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?text=TestSharedInformerHandlerAbuse

I'm not entirely happy with "it's a bit slower" without a clear explanation why. I'll keep looking.

Taking a quick look as well to see what might be the cause, also there have been a number of changes to shared informers. One that is top of mind is us removing the mutex lock while processing (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136264), while I doubt that is the cause, this is not the only PR that affects this portion of the codebase. Do we know where it panics?

I went through every single goroutine in the panic dump after a timeout:

[timeout.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25610752/timeout.log)

Many goroutines are blocked trying to add or remove an event handler, trying to acquire `s.startedLock`. What isn't obvious to me is which goroutine is currently *holding* it. Maybe none, and if we were to let the goroutines continue they would make progress?

Strange that it fails after 5m though looking at https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?text=TestSharedInformerHandlerAbuse... That should be more than enough time for this to progress though right?

It also times out with fdcbb6cba9a04c028b158bf66d505df7431f63fe, the commit prior to 5ff323de791df88880f6e065f5de4b445e5c90ed.

For correctness, that one needs a fix that should have been included in that commit and not the one about informer factory:

```patch
diff --git a/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go b/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go
index 503cd2e2dac..f61589151d3 100644
--- a/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go
+++ b/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go
@@ -888,6 +888,10 @@ func (s *sharedIndexInformer) AddEventHandlerWithOptions(handler ResourceEventHa
                // thread adding them and the counter is temporarily zero).
                listener.add(addNotification{newObj: item, isInInitialList: true})
        }
+
+       // Initial list is added, now we can allow the listener to detect that "upstream has synced".
+       s.processor.wg.Start(listener.watchSynced)
+
        return handle, nil
 }
 
@@ -1008,7 +1012,8 @@ func (p *sharedProcessor) addListener(listener *processorListener) ResourceEvent
        p.listeners[listener] = true
 
        if p.listenersStarted {
-               p.wg.Start(listener.watchSynced)
+               // Not starting listener.watchSynced!
+               // The caller must first add the initial list, then start it.
                p.wg.Start(listener.run)
                p.wg.Start(listener.pop)
        }
```

I was able to repro it I think

```
func (p *sharedProcessor) run(ctx context.Context) {
	func() {
		hook := sharedProcessorRunHook.Load()
		if hook != nil {
			(*hook)()
		}
         --->time.Sleep(3 * time.Second)
		// Changing listenersStarted needs a write lock.
		p.listenersLock.Lock()
		defer p.listenersLock.Unlock()
		for listener := range p.listeners {
			p.wg.Start(listener.watchSynced)
			p.wg.Start(listener.run)
			p.wg.Start(listener.pop)
		}
		p.listenersStarted = true
		p.listenersRCond.Signal()
	}()
	<-ctx.Done()
```

Adding this time.Sleep triggered the issue immediately. The deadlock occurs because watchSynced goroutines are unconditionally spawned by AddEventHandlerWithOptions, even though sharedProcessor.run has not started yet. I think @pohly's change caused this to happen quickly enough that we can get stuck in this spot. Not sure what the best way to fix this is.


The above PR seems to resolve it, I intentionally added a delay to ensure it passes now. However I think we can take advantage of the existing hook that @pohly added here for testing. Still not to familiar with synctest to add one but I can take a look later/ if someone else wants to :)

> If this was a genuine bug like a deadlock, then it should also fail with a higher timeout.

That argument was flawed: without an explicit `-test.timeout`, a test binary runs without any timeout, so `stress` didn't report anything because no test binary had failed - any binary in the deadlock would just keep running. Even if the default 10 minute timeout had been active, I didn't even wait long enough for that.

TLDR: always use `stress` with `-test.timeout`!

Thanks @akhilerm for reporting the problem and bisecting it.
